title: Satya Nadella predicts AI agents will reshuffle the economics of the web
content:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella predicts that the rise of AI agents is going to reshape the economics of the internet, impacting the business models of the companies that rely on advertising and what he referred to as “human web” traffic.
Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the tech executive argued that the shift to an agentic web could change which companies pay others for traffic and for transactions, similar to how the transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google did years ago.
“The current aggregators who have a business model which was for the human web will get, in some sense, reshuffled,” said Nadella. “And if you were monetizing ads because of the eyeballs, you now have to probably get down to essentially maybe CPC [cost-per-click] wins; maybe it’s more transactional,” he continued. “And so if you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will.”
The discussion turned to Amazon and its decision to block AI agents from accessing its retail website, preventing them from browsing its catalog and making purchases on behalf of their users. Nadella suggested that companies trying to protect their existing business models could lose out to others that are more willing to embrace the AI agents. For instance, if Amazon continues blocking agents, another shopping platform such as Shopify, could allow them, and gain an advantage.
“I think this is going to be interesting,” he said, speaking to the changing models. “It’s the same thing that’s happening in other categories, right? Which is, if you’re in love with a particular business model, you have to kind of scramble,” he said.

report.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says AI agents will reshuffle the internet's economics, forcing ad-funded platforms to rethink traffic and transaction models or risk being displaced by rivals that embrace agents.
report.background: The web's economy has long rested on a simple bargain: platforms aggregate human attention, then monetize it through advertising or referrals. Nadella frames agentic AI as the next structural break of that model — comparable to the shift from portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google, which reallocated who paid whom for traffic. The tension is already visible: Amazon has blocked third-party AI agents from browsing its catalog and buying on users' behalf, protecting its storefront and ad business. Meanwhile, agent-friendly commerce infrastructure is maturing fast, with payment protocols from Google and OpenAI/Stripe, and merchant-side tooling from Shopify. Publishers face a parallel squeeze as AI summaries reduce click-throughs, prompting pay-per-crawl schemes and licensing deals. The core question is no longer whether agents will transact on the web, but which intermediaries capture the value — and whether incumbents' defenses become their own disruption.
key_points: Nadella argues agents will 'reshuffle' today's aggregators, much as search engines displaced portals. Companies monetizing eyeballs through ads may need to shift toward cost-per-click or transactional revenue, because agent-mediated traffic behaves differently from human browsing: fewer page views, more completed tasks and purchases.

He warned that blocking agents is a risky defensive move. If Amazon keeps AI agents off its storefront, an agent-permitted rival like Shopify could capture those purchases instead. The implication: refusing agents may protect short-term ad revenue while ceding long-term transaction volume.

The economics of who pays whom for traffic are up for renegotiation. Under the 'human web,' platforms paid for clicks and referrals; in an agentic web, payments may flow per transaction, per API call, or per piece of licensed content, changing the leverage of publishers, merchants and intermediaries.

Nadella's blunt advice to incumbents: 'if you don't accept the agent, somebody else will.' He described a scramble for companies attached to a single business model, suggesting adaptation speed — not scale — will decide who keeps their position in the value chain.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this legitimizes agentic commerce as the next platform war: model providers, payment networks and merchants are racing to own the protocol layer where agents browse and pay. Expect more tension over access — bot-blocking, pay-per-crawl, and licensing deals will become standard negotiating tools. For developers, the practical shift is toward building agent-accessible interfaces: structured product data, machine-readable permissions and payment APIs, rather than pages designed purely for human eyes. For regular users, agents promise convenience — delegated shopping, booking and research — but also less visible choice architecture, since the agent, not the user, decides which merchant gets the click. The near-term risk is a fragmented web where some sites welcome agents and others wall them off.
report.tools: Watch Google's AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) and OpenAI/Stripe's Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) for agent-initiated checkout; Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the standard for connecting agents to tools and data; Cloudflare's pay-per-crawl and Web Bot Auth for bot verification and monetization; Shopify's agentic commerce tooling for merchants; and llms.txt plus robots.txt-adjacent content-signal specs for declaring how AI agents may use a site.
